items.title: Digital Literacy as a Predictor of AI Literacy: A Gender Paradox and a Knowledge–Belief Gap
items.abstract: This study investigates the relationship between university students’ digital literacy and artificial intelligence (AI) literacy. Participants were 770 undergraduate students (227 male, 543 female; Mage = 21.27, SD = 2.75) recruited through online convenience and snowball sampling, with recruitment centered at Karamanoğlu Mehmetbey University (Karaman, Türkiye), representing more than 120 academic programs. Data were collected with the Turkish forms of Ng’s (2012) Digital Literacy Scale (α = .931) and Wang et al.’s (2022) AI Literacy Scale (α = .803). Three findings stand out. First, digital literacy and AI literacy were strongly and positively related (r = .596, p < .001). A three-step hierarchical regression analysis identified digital literacy as the only significant predictor of AI literacy (β = .599, p < .001), explaining 35.5% of the variance (R² = .355, F(1, 768) = 422.57, p < .001); adding gender and age (ΔR² = .002) and internet use frequency (ΔR² = .000) did not significantly improve the model. Second, a small gender difference favoring men emerged in digital literacy (Cohen’s d = 0.201) but not in AI literacy (d = 0.031), a pattern we describe as a gender paradox. Third, although 85.1% of participants believed in AI’s future impact, only 22.7% rated their own AI knowledge as sufficient—a knowledge–belief gap. Self-rated AI knowledge, but not belief, differed significantly by gender (χ² = 11.05, p = .004; Cramér’s V = .120). Implications for digital and AI literacy education in higher education are discussed.

items.abstract: Abstract The advent of the digital age has significantly reshaped human relationships, modes of communication, identity formation, education, culture, and literary creation. In the Indian context, the proliferation of the internet, social media, smartphones, digital publishing, and artificial intelligence has revolutionized not just daily existence but also how literature is produced and consumed. Indian English literature, traditionally responsive to societal transformations, has increasingly addressed the conflicts arising from globalization, technological advancement, consumerism, urbanization, social disparity, and evolving patterns of human interaction. This paper explores how human values are portrayed and reconfigured in contemporary Indian English literature within the framework of digital modernity. It contends that literature remains a crucial ethical domain for interrogating issues such as dignity, empathy, equality, truth, identity, liberty, responsibility, and interpersonal relations. Representative works including Aravind Adiga's The White Tiger and Selection Day are analyzed to understand the interplay between technological progress and human values. Furthermore, the paper examines the growth of digital literary forms in India, such as digital literature, blogs, online literary forums, social media writing, and electronic literature. The study concludes that while digital technology has broadened the scope of Indian English literature, it has also introduced new ethical dilemmas. The enduring relevance of literature resides in its ability to keep human dignity and moral inquiry at the heart of technological change. items.abstract: Abstract Because of the advent of the digital era, human relationship, communication, human identity, learning, culture, and literature have all changed. With the advent of the Internet, social media, smart phones, digital publishing and artificial intelligence, the way people read and write literature in India has changed greatly, impacting everyday life. Indian English literature has always been sensitive towards the changes in society and now it is venturing forth to face the type of conflicts that globalization, technological development, consumerism, urbanization, social inequality and different relationship between humans and humans have introduced to the world. The present paper tries to speak on the representation and reconstruction of human values in the Indian English literature in the context of digital modernity. It asserts that literature is still an important moral territory to question dignity, empathy, equality, truth, identity, freedom, responsibility and human relationships. In the representative works presented, The White Tiger by Aravind Adiga and Selection Day, technological advancement and human values are explored. Moreover, the paper discusses the development of literary forms in the digital realm in India including digital literature, blogs, online literary platforms and forums, social media writing and electronic literature. Finally, a conclusion is provided on how digital technology has expanded the field of Indian English literature and how it has created new ethical dilemmas. The ability of literature to be relevant is to always keep the human dignity and ethics as the focus of technological development. In the digital age, human interactions, communication, identity formation, education, culture and literary creation has been radically changed. In terms of literature, the internet, social media, smart phones, digital publishing and AI have changed the face of the Indian landscape, not just in the ways in which we live, but in how we create and consume books. The Indian English literature, which traditionally responds to changes in the society, has taken an increasing interest in the issues of conflicts and challenges emerging out of globalization, technology, consumerism, urbanization, social inequality, and changing patterns of human interactions.

items.title: Digital Twin Technology in Pharmaceutical Manufacturing
items.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology is an emerging digital technogy that is gaining importance in modern pharmaceutical manufacturing. It creates a virtual representation of a physical machine, process, product, or manufacturing facility and connects it with real-time information from the actual system. In pharmaceutical manufacturing, data from sensors, manufacturing equipment, and Process Analytical Technology (PAT) can be combined with mathematical, statistical, mechan istic, and data-driven models to understand how a process behaves. This helps manufacturers monitor processes continuously, identify changes at an early stage, and maintain consistent product quality. Digital Twin technology can be used in different pharmaceutical operations such as mixing, granulation, drying, tablet compression, coating, filling, and packaging. It also has potential applications in biopharmaceutical processes such as cell culture, fermentation, filtration, and purification. One of the major benefits of a digital twin is that it allows manufacturers to observe and analyze a process without depending only on physical testing. It can also be used to study different process conditions virtually before making changes to the actual manufacturing process. This may help in process optimization and reduce unnecessary experiments. Digital twins can support Quality by Design (QbD) by improving the understanding of the relationship between raw materials, process parameters, and critical quality attributes. They are also useful in continuous manufacturing, where large amounts of real-time process data are generated. Another important application is predictive maintenance, where equipment data can be analyzed to identify unusual changes and possible equipment failures before they occur. When digital twins are combined with PAT, artificial intelligence, machine learning, Internet of Things (IoT), and cloud computing, they can provide more detailed information about pharmaceutical processes and support the development of Pharma 4.0. Digital twins may also support real-time release testing, process optimization, manufacturing simulation, and predictive quality management. However, several challenges need to be considered before their widespread use. These include data quality, data integrity, model accuracy, system interoperability, cybersecurity, high implementation costs, model validation, and regulatory requirements. Pharmaceutical manufacturing also requires strict control and documentation, so digital-twin models used for important manufacturing or quality decisions need to be properly validated and maintained. In addition, successful implementation requires cooperation between pharmaceutical scientists, engineers, data scientists, IT professionals, and quality-control teams. Human involvement is still important because professionals need to understand the information provided by the digital twin and make appropriate decisions. Although digital twin technology is still developing, it has considerable potential to improve pharmaceutical manufacturing by supporting better process understanding, real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, process optimization, and quality management. Future developments are expected to focus on better integration with artificial intelligence, continuous manufacturing, advanced analytical technologies, and automated manufacturing systems. Overall, Digital Twin technology can play an important role in the digital transformation of pharmaceutical manufacturing and may contribute to more efficient, consistent, flexible, and data-driven production.[1-5]

items.title: Digital-Age Ethics for Elementary Teachers: Challenges and Strategies for Professional Integrity
items.abstract: Digital transformation has expanded elementary teachers’ work into learning platforms, social media, messaging applications, data systems, and generative artificial intelligence. These tools support collaboration and instructional improvement but raise ethical concerns about professional boundaries, children’s privacy and safety, information integrity, copyright, equity, and accountability. This article synthesizes the ethical challenges faced by elementary school teachers in digital environments and identifies strategies for maintaining professional integrity while prioritizing children’s best interests. A narrative literature review was conducted through exploratory searches of scholarly articles, academic books, international frameworks, policy documents, and Indonesian legislation, prioritizing publications from 2020 to 2026 alongside foundational theories. The thematic synthesis identifies risks involving blurred personal and professional boundaries, children’s data governance, unsafe online communication, unverified digital and AI-generated content, and unequal access to technology. It proposes a Five-Dimension Framework of Teachers’ Digital Integrity comprising pedagogical, relational, information-and-data, epistemic, and civic-professional integrity. Recommendations are directed to teachers, schools, teacher education programs, families, and professional associations. The framework is a conceptual synthesis, not a validated instrument, and requires empirical testing in Indonesian elementary schools

items.title: Drawbacks and Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in the Medical Field
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become an important technology in modern healthcare. It is being used for medical image analysis, disease prediction, clinical decision support, drug discovery, patient monitoring, and administrative activities. AI can improve the speed and efficiency of healthcare, but its use also introduces significant risks. This paper examines the major drawbacks of AI in the medical field, including algorithmic bias, inaccurate predictions, lack of explainability, privacy and security risks, high implementation costs, overdependence on automated systems, accountability problems, and lack of quality training data, ethical concerns, and unequal access to AI-based healthcare. The World Health Organization (WHO) has specifically emphasized the importance of safety, transparency, human autonomy, accountability, equity, and privacy when implementing AI in healthcare. The paper also discusses possible solutions and future research directions for developing safe, reliable, and responsible medical AI.

items.title: Dynamic prediction of extra-corporal circuit clotting risk during hemodialysis sessions using deep learning: a retrospective study
items.abstract: Extra-corporal circuit (ECC) clotting during hemodialysis (HD) is a well-known issue that is hard to detect early, potentially leading to blood loss and reduced treatment duration. Ideally, clotting should be detected in time to administer additional anticoagulants or initiate restitution. However, most studies focus on finding the ideal anticoagulation strategy without the support of any data-driven solution. This study aims to develop an Artificial Intelligence model for dynamic ECC clotting-risk prediction using in-session temporal monitoring data (main data) and patients’ out-session clinical data (contextual data), with the goal of providing early alerts. The model is trained to predict the risk that a dialysis session will end with clotting-related outcome, rather than to detect clot formation at a specific time point. Leveraging Deep Learning for dynamic prediction, this study experiments with Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) architecture and two contextual LSTM approaches (concatenation and multiplication) to identify the best-fitting architecture. The impact of incorporating patients’ out-of-session clinical data is also assessed by testing an LSTM without these features. Data were collected from electronic records at Reims University Hospital (2015–2021), covering 113,119 sessions with 47 in-session and 28 out-session features. Performance differences between models were minimal. The final model, LSTM with raw concatenation of in- and out-session data, reached an F1-Score of 0.8 and an area under the ROC curve of 0.89 for session-end prediction. In a simulated clinical evaluation using sequential predictions, that model surpassed an F1-Score of 0.67 only after two hours of session time had elapsed (sensitivity: 0.7, precision: 0.64), out of an average session length of four hours. Strong performance in session-end prediction suggests dynamic clotting-risk prediction is feasible with Deep Learning. However, early-session predictions remain challenging, likely due to the granularity of clotting annotations in the study. These results provide a solid foundation for further advancements.

items.title: Dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in the educational process: Assessment based on the analysis of biometric indicators under various formats of academic workload
items.abstract: Introduction. The article addresses the problem of declining cognitive engagement among students in the educational process, which negatively affects the quality of professional preparation and the formation of required competencies. Traditional methods of analysis (surveys, observation) do not allow obtaining an objective picture of the dynamics of the cognitive state during a lesson, which complicates scientifically grounded design of the educational process. The purpose of this article is to identify patterns in the dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in various formats of educational activities based on the analysis of biometric indicators. Materials and Methods. The study was conducted at the National Research Tomsk Polytechnic University during the spring semester of the 2025/2026 academic year (sample N=120). A pedagogical experiment (action research) was carried out with the participation of 120 senior students. Continuously recorded biometric parameters (heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, and skin temperature) were used as objective indicators of engagement. For integral assessment, a weighted engagement index was calculated. ANOVA, Student’s t-test, and Pearson correlation analysis were applied. Results. The authors identified statistically significant differences in students’ physiological reactions depending on the format of educational activities: practical classes cause maximum activation (index 0.78), while lectures cause minimum activation (0.42). A cyclic dynamics of attention during a 90-minute lesson was established, with a characteristic drop in concentration in the middle of the class. It was proven that the cyclic structure of the lesson prevents this dip through the alternation of work formats. It was experimentally confirmed that the introduction of the cyclic lesson structure significantly (p < 0.001) increases the integral engagement index (up to 0.76) and ensures better knowledge retention. Students in the experimental group outperformed students in the control group by 27 points when testing residual knowledge after 14-day period. Conclusions. The identified patterns in the dynamics of students’ cognitive engagement in various formats of educational activities (lecture, practical class, project work) based on the analysis of biometric indicators create a scientific basis for designing classes synchronized with the natural cycles of brain performance. The proposed lesson structure facilitates the transition from passive perception of information to active cognitive activities and the formation of sustainable knowledge.

items.title: Edge AI for Energy-Efficient Smart IoT Systems: A Sustainable Computing Approach
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence of Things (AIoT) is transforming Internet of Things (IoT) systems by enabling data-driven decisions close to the point where data are generated. However, conventional cloud-centric architectures can introduce communication overhead, latency, privacy concerns, and additional energy costs. This paper examines Edge AI as a sustainable computing approach for energy-efficient smart IoT systems, with particular relevance to the development priorities associated with Viksit Bharat 2047. The study follows a descriptive and analytical approach based on research literature concerning TinyML, on-device machine learning, Edge AI, and energy-aware IoT. It proposes an architecture consisting of sensing, local inference, edge coordination, selective cloud processing, and energy-aware orchestration. The paper further identifies measurable parameters including accuracy, inference latency, energy per inference, communication volume, memory footprint, and reliability for evaluating sustainable AIoT systems. The objective is not to claim unverified experimental results, but to establish a practical research framework that can subsequently be tested on resource-constrained edge hardware. The study indicates that sustainable AIoT should be evaluated not only through predictive performance but also through the computational, communication, and energy resources required to deliver each intelligent decision.

items.title: Educloud: Development of an Integrated Digital Learning Platform Based on Cloud Computing, LMS, Artificial Intelligence, and Edupreneurship
items.abstract: This study evaluated the initial feasibility and practicality of Educloud, a cloud-based digital learning platform integrating Learning Management System functions, digital assessment, learner-progress monitoring, and an AI-supported Edupreneurship workflow. Educloud was developed using Laravel and PostgreSQL, with AI functionality provided through the Google Gemini Developer API using the gemini-2.5-flash model. The AI component processes pseudonymised learner and team profiles to generate business-idea recommendations and formative feedback. The study employed a research and development approach based on an adapted ADDIE model, involving three expert validators and ten users in a small-group trial. Functional testing assessed API connectivity, contextual-data processing, privacy protection, response validation, storage, and error handling. Expert validation produced a score of 489 out of 525 (93.14%), a mean of 4.66, and an Aiken’s V of 0.91. The small-group trial produced a score of 1,117 out of 1,250 (89.36%), a mean of 4.47, and a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.93. The findings indicate that Educloud demonstrates strong initial feasibility and practicality. Further field testing is required to evaluate the accuracy of AI-generated recommendations and their effects on learning and Edupreneurship outcomes.

items.title: Emerging Perspective in English Language, Literature and Communication
items.abstract: The intersection of English language teaching, literary studies, and communication studies in light of the ongoing digital revolution. Using the results of a comprehensive literature review (2021-2026) and comparative analysis, the paper outlines three key emerging paradigms: artificial intelligence in language teaching, the digital and environmental turns in literary theory, and the transition from consequence to emergence in communication studies. Mixed-methodology, including both qualitative content analysis and quantitative bibliometric indicators, will be used in order to delineate the intersections. It is found that while each field has its unique pattern of technological integration, there is an important common focus on ethical governance, learner/user agency, and interdisciplinary cooperation. It is argued that in order to ensure sustainable development of the respective fields, it is crucial to introduce critical digital literacy into all three areas along with supportive institutional structures for AI implementation.

items.abstract: Abstract New technologies have a significant impact on language learning process. The traditional language learning is largely based on textbooks, classroom teaching, blackboard and face-to-face communication. Digital technologies now offer learners new opportunities to learn, practise, communicate and assess their language proficiency. New opportunities for language education emerge in the fields of Artificial Intelligence (AI), mobile applications, virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), chatbots, speech-recognition systems, learning management systems, online platforms, digital games, and adaptive learning systems. The technologies help to create flexible, interactive, personalised and learner-centred experiences for learners. The scope of this research paper is to explore the significant emerging technologies in language learning and talk about their applications, advantages, problems and significance in language learning. The paper makes the case that technology isn't a substitute for teachers. Rather, it supports educators, and provides extra opportunities for effective language use. The theme, which seeks to redefine the language learning landscape, was well-received, and attendees eagerly explored the diverse methods and approaches for incorporating emerging technologies into language education. The theme was well-received, and participants welcomed the opportunity to discuss various methods and approaches for integrating emerging technologies into language learning. items.title: Enhancing Infectious Disease Prediction in Slum Areas using a Sustainable Approach with Backpropagation Algorithm
items.abstract: Developing countries continue to grapple with the burden of infectious diseases in managing their public health.The growing use of technology and machine learning in healthcare has seen significant adoption of diagnostic and predictive ML models mostly in developed countries with enough supportive resources.For resource-constrained countries with substantial populations living in informal settlements, there has been a growing need for the integration of ML in their healthcare management.In response, we design a sustainable machine learning model for improving the prediction of infectious diseases in informal settlements.We strive to address limitations of existing predictive models, particularly their inability to effectively handle noisy, incomplete, and resourceconstrained datasets common in slum environments.The research is handled in phases with this paper covering the first objective which aims at understanding the prevalence of infectious diseases and existing management strategies in informal settlements of Kibera, Mathare, and Mukuru kwa Njenga in Nairobi, Kenya.To achieve this, we adopt a mixed-methods research design to investigate the distribution and management of infectious diseases in selected areas.The subsequent phases of the research will evaluate existing machine learning datasets, and finally develop and evaluate a setting-specific ANN-based predictive model.The model will be trained using the backpropagation algorithm with stochastic gradient descent optimization and evaluated using standard machine learning performance metrics, including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrix analysis.In the first phase, the paper confirms high prevalence of Tuberculosis, Malaria, Cholera and HIV/AIDs, as well as existing management strategies adopted and the challenges in informal settlement.The proposed framework is expected to improve predictive accuracy by learning complex nonlinear relationships between clinical symptoms, environmental conditions, and socio-demographic factors.While we acknowledge that infectious diseases remain a serious health challenge in informal settlements, we believe that the proposed model provides a promising approach for developing sustainable, scalable, and cost-effective infectious disease prediction systems tailored to informal settlements.Future implementation should further validate the model using real-world clinical and community datasets, integrate it with existing health information systems, and continuously retrain it using updated epidemiological data.Policymakers should also support digital health infrastructure and standardized data collection to enhance predictive healthcare in informal settlements.This research contributes to the growing application of artificial intelligence in public health by demonstrating how optimized backpropagation-based neural networks can support sustainable infectious disease prediction in resource-constrained environments.

items.title: Entre el error y el eco: estéticas de la interfaz en la era de la IA generativa
items.abstract: In an era shaped by ecological collapse, technological displacement, and social fragmentation, Zeitgeist25 investigates digital art as a surface onto which collective anxiety is projected. A “melancholic” machine —left behind after humanity’s disappearance— grapples with a longing embedded in its own code. Drawing on glitch aesthetics, generative AI, and conceptual dramaturgy, the work reframes system errors and technical commands as expressive gestures of vulnerability, persistence, and failure. Unfolding across four poetic acts, each section traces the machine’s attempt to “comprehend” the absence of its creators and to situate itself within a world devoid of human reference. Rather than attributing genuine emotion to artificial intelligence, simulated longing operates as a theatrical device, exposing emotional projections, contemporary fears, and cultural tensions. By staging collapse, the work becomes both critique and catharsis: a document of the 2025 zeitgeist, where the boundaries between system and soul, error and expression, simulation and sincerity begin to blur, confronting the viewer with their own technological fragility.

items.title: Epistemic IR as the Missing Meta-Tool
items.abstract: Knowledge systems do more than store propositions. They decide what may count as a claim, which evidence may support it, whose judgment may alter its standing, when uncertainty requires deferment, and how decisions can be contested or revised. Those governance commitments are usually distributed across prose, software, institutional practice, standards, and tacit authority. This paper develops Epistemic Intermediate Representation (Epistemic IR) as a candidate representation profile for making that machinery explicit. An Epistemic IR artifact binds an exact claim to its interpretation, scope, epistemic posture, standing, provenance, evidence, applicable standards, authority dependencies, adjudication state, contest history, and revision lineage. An external, versioned admission regime may evaluate the artifact and emit a bounded decision receipt. The representation does not decide truth, manufacture authority, or make a receipt self-validating. Corpus-wide comparison produces an important compression. MCIR already proposes a canonical intermediate representation for governed transformation. Constitutional Epistemics, Epistemic Authority Governance, Epistemic Situational Awareness, Admissibility Engineering, reasoning receipts, and the Governed Knowledge Loop already supply much of the governance machinery. Epistemic IR should therefore remain a candidate epistemic profile of MCIR unless it demonstrates semantics or conformance obligations that the general representation cannot express. Its strongest present contribution is not another foundational substrate, but a portable claim-governance profile that makes admission, refusal, deferment, contest, and revision inspectable without confusing procedural standing with truth.

items.title: Epistemic Situational Awareness and the Governed Knowledge Loop
items.abstract: Reasoning systems can generate claims faster than they can preserve source identity, evidentiary standing, contradiction, authority, uncertainty, and revision history. Epistemic Situational Awareness (ESA) addresses the local problem: what posture does a proposed reasoning act occupy now, and what continuations are permitted? The Governed Knowledge Loop (GKL) addresses the temporal problem: how do observations, claims, evidence, relationships, decisions, and revisions enter and evolve within a knowledge system without silently acquiring stronger standing? This paper integrates ESA and GKL as complementary capabilities of governed semantic infrastructure. ESA is defined operationally as an evidence-qualified representation of a system's epistemic position, not introspective certainty or human-like awareness. GKL is defined as a typed lifecycle whose outcomes include admission, qualification, conflict, refusal, deferral, supersession, archival, and unknown. Together they can make claim promotion and continuation more inspectable when their instrumentation, enforcement, and evidence actually cover the relevant path. The result is an architecture and evaluation program. It does not establish truth, knowledge stability, AI safety, institutional legitimacy, or a working implementation.

items.title: Ergonomic Risk and Musculoskeletal Disorders in Computer Users: A ROSA-NMQ Literature Review
items.abstract: The increasing use of computers, predominantly involving prolonged static sitting, may increase the risk of musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs). This study aims to examine workstation ergonomic risk and musculoskeletal disorders among computer users through a literature review based on the Rapid Office Strain Assessment (ROSA) and the Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire (NMQ). A systematic search was conducted in PubMed and Google Scholar for articles published between 2020 and 2025, following PRISMA guidelines. A total of nine studies that met the inclusion criteria were analyzed narratively. The results indicate that most studies reported moderate to high levels of ergonomic risk, with chair-related factors as the dominant contributors. The prevalence of musculoskeletal complaints was also high, particularly in the neck, shoulders, and lower back. However, the relationship between ROSA scores and musculoskeletal complaints was inconsistent across studies, suggesting the influence of multifactorial determinants. Therefore, ROSA is more appropriately used as a screening tool for ergonomic risk, while NMQ complements it by capturing subjective complaints. The combined use of both instruments is essential to support a more comprehensive ergonomic assessment and the development of effective interventions.

items.title: Ergonomics, Kaizen and Organisational Support as Pathways to Worker Well-Being in Malaysian Automotive Manufacturing: A Conceptual Framework and Research Design
items.abstract: Automotive production in Malaysia is being reshaped by automation and Industry 4.0, yet manual and semi-automated assembly work continues to expose production workers to physical strain, time pressure and the demands of continuous improvement programmes. Studies of ergonomics and Kaizen have largely developed in parallel, and the psychosocial mechanisms through which both might influence worker well-being have been rarely tested. This paper develops an integrative conceptual framework and a research design to address that gap. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources theory, Organisational Support Theory, and Social Exchange Theory, the framework proposes that physical ergonomic factors and Kaizen practices influence worker well-being directly and indirectly, with perceived organisational support as a mediating mechanism. Five hypotheses are developed from the existing theoretical and empirical literature. A quantitative cross-sectional design is then specified for production and technical workers at automotive industry and its vendors in Tanjung Malim, Perak, covering the target population, a minimum sample of 361 respondents, a 40-item reflective measurement instrument, content and face validation, a 30-respondent pilot test and a two-step partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) analysis. This paper contributes a testable model that links technical and operational practices to Worker Well-Being through a psychosocial pathway, and it offers a replicable protocol for researchers studying production workers in comparable manufacturing settings. No empirical results are reported; the paper sets out the model and the design against which the main study will be evaluated.

items.title: Ethical Values and Their Significance in the Present Scenario
items.abstract: Abstract: Ethical values constitute the moral foundation of human behavior, shaping actions, decisions, and relationships in both personal and collective life. In the modern era—characterized by technological advancement, globalization, and social complexity—ethical principles are essential for promoting justice, accountability, and sustainable progress. Rooted in ancient philosophical and religious traditions, ethics has long guided humanity toward harmony and social order. Thinkers such as Aristotle and Confucius, along with sacred texts like the 'Bhagavad Gita', emphasized virtues such as honesty, integrity, and responsibility, which remain universally relevant. Ethical values, broadly defined as standards that distinguish right from wrong, operate at multiple levels: personal, social, and organizational. Core principles—honesty, integrity, fairness, respect, and responsibility—form the moral compass that governs ethical decision-making and fosters trust within communities and institutions. These principles ensure equitable treatment, accountability, and respect for human dignity. However, the contemporary world presents new ethical challenges. Artificial intelligence, digital media, and biotechnology raise issues of privacy, bias, and misuse. Globalization demands sensitivity to cultural diversity, while climate change underscores moral responsibility toward future generations. Corporate malpractices and corruption further highlight the need for ethical awareness and moral leadership. Ethical values are therefore vital for personal integrity, social harmony, and responsible governance. They strengthen individual character, promote inclusivity, and guide organizations toward transparent and sustainable practices. At the global level, ethical awareness supports human rights, environmental protection, and cooperative problem-solving.In conclusion, ethical values remain indispensable for ensuring balance between progress and moral responsibility. They guide humanity toward a just, compassionate, and sustainable world—where technological, social, and economic development align with the enduring principles of integrity, fairness, and respect.

items.title: Evaluating AI Disclosure Practices and Regulatory Gaps in Quantitative Finance
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes increasingly prominent within financial markets, regulators lack the frameworks necessary to assess whether AI-driven investment strategies comply with fiduciary standards, manage systemic risk responsibly, or produce returns through legitimate means. This gap is particularly prevalent among leading quantitative trading and investment firms, which deploy sophisticated machine learning systems while simultaneously disclosing little about how those systems are built or monitored. This paper analyzes the publicly available AI disclosure practices and performance of five major quantitative trading and investment firms (Renaissance Technologies, Two Sigma, D. E. Shaw, Citadel, and Jane Street) from Q1 2023 to Q1 2026, comparing returns from their publicly disclosed top-20 equity holdings against the S&P 500 using data from the website HedgeFollow. The findings reveal that all five firms score below 40 out of 100 on a disclosure rubric created for this study, with the largest gaps appearing in model governance, retraining procedures, risk limits, stress-response behavior, and incident-reporting protocols. At the same time, three firms—Renaissance Technologies, D. E. Shaw, and Jane Street—display peak cumulative return gaps ranging from approximately 40 to over 100 percentage points above the S&P 500 during the study period, demonstrating that strong performance can coexist with limited public visibility into the systems and controls behind that performance. items.abstract: Evidence based prosthodontics (EBP) integrates the best available scientific evidence with clinical expertise and patient values. Prosthodontics includes long-established procedures, interventions supported by varying levels of evidence and rapidly developing technologies. A critical evidence- based approach is needed to distinguish demonstrated clinical benefit from tradition, laboratory findings and technological enthusiasm.This narrative review presents a broad, clinically oriented synthesis of evidence across complete dentures, removable partial dentures, fixed prosthodontics, occlusion, temporomandibular disorders, implant prosthodontics, implant overdentures, full-arch rehabilitation, peri - implant health, bone augmentation, contemporary biomaterials, CAD/CAM, digital dentures, additive manufacturing, artificial intelligence, patient reported outcomes and maintenance. The McGill Consensus of 2002 and York Consensus of 2009 are discussed as important milestones within implant prosthodontics rather than as the central theme of EBP.3,4,5 Current evidence supports two-implant mandibular overdentures as a highly effective option for many edentulous patients, while treatment must remain individualized.

items.title: Evolution of artificial intelligence in education from technology adoption to ethical governance and educator preparedness
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) reshapes teaching, learning, and administration, educators face pedagogical, ethical, and professional challenges. This study maps the structure, themes, and research trends of AI-in-education scholarship using bibliometric and quantitative content analysis. Using the PRISMA protocol for search and screening, 208 peer-reviewed articles from the Scopus database, published between 2021 and 2025, were retrieved, and analysed using Biblioshiny (Bibliometrix 5.5.0; R 4.6.1) and VOSviewer 1.6.21. The field is expanding rapidly, with 8 articles in 2021 and 106 in 2025 (90.79% annual growth rate). Science mapping (keyword co-occurrence, bibliographic coupling, and co-citation) indicates that the field is grounded in technology-acceptance and self-efficacy theory, and features convergence around generative AI, AI literacy, and ethical application. A thematic map places educational technology and ChatGPT among motor themes and generative AI among emerging themes. A complementary content analysis of all 208 articles yields six thematic categories, the largest being students’ AI literacy, perceptions, and learning with AI tools (25.0%), AI in health-professions and other disciplinary education (21.2%), and human–AI learning frameworks (19.2%). Ethics and responsible-AI terms appear in about 40% of the articles, adoption terms in 30%, and educator-preparedness terms in 36%. The results indicate that responsible AI use is a prominent strand of the field, and give guidelines for policy, institutional leadership, faculty development and future research. The findings inform AI-in-education scholarship and educational policy aligned with United Nations Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4).

items.title: Evolution of Artificial Intelligence Models and Agents: A Survey and Future Research Directions
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is all about building the systems that can observe the world carefully,think about it, learn through experience and completely the task accurately. In the last decade, progress in data, computing power and neural network architectures has produced powerful AI models, especially deep learning systems, transformers and large language models (LLMs). Building on these models, a new class of systems called AI agents can pursue goals autonomously by planning, using tools, remembering context and acting on their environment. This paper reviews the foundations of AI, the major types of AI models, the architecture and types of AI agents, their applications across sectors, and the challenges of safety, bias, privacy and governance that accompany them.

items.title: Examining Teachers’ Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence and Technostress Levels
items.abstract: Technostress refers to stress associated with the use of technology. Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to technologies that enable computer systems to perform tasks commonly associated with human intelligence. In recent years, AI has been used in many areas such as problem solving, speech processing, image recognition and image classification, and its use in education has become increasingly widespread. Against this background, the study examined teachers’ attitudes towards AI and their technostress levels. Within the scope of the research, a quantitative relational survey design was employed, and the sample consisted of 319 teachers working in schools affiliated with the Ministry of National Education in Türkiye. Data were collected using the General Attitudes towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (GAAIS) and the Teachers’ Techno-stress Levels Defining Scale (TTLDS). The findings revealed that teachers reported high levels of positive attitudes towards AI, moderate levels of negative attitudes, and moderate levels of technostress. The data analysis indicated a moderate positive relationship between teachers’ technostress levels and their general attitudes towards AI. In addition, teachers’ AI attitude scores differed significantly by education level and teaching branch but not by gender or age. It was also found that teachers’ scores on the technostress scale differed by gender, age and branch but not by education level.

items.title: Expert-based classification on the technical difficulty of single-port urological robotic procedures
items.abstract: Single-port (SP) robotic surgery represents the latest paradigm shift in minimally invasive urology. Despite its progressive adoption worldwide, no structured classification of procedural difficulty exists for SP urological procedures. We aimed to develop an expert-based scoring system to grade the technical difficulty of urological procedures performed with the da Vinci SP platform. A questionnaire-based expert-consensus study was conducted during an international meeting on SP robotic surgery (Turin, Italy, February 2026). Consensus here refers to the descriptive convergence of independent, single-round ratings rather than a formal iterative (e.g., Delphi) consensus process. Eligible experts had independent or assisted SP robotic experience. Using a structured questionnaire, they rated each procedure on three dimensions - technical difficulty, operative risk and sustained attention required - on a 7-point Likert scale. A composite difficulty score was obtained by summing the three median values. Experts also estimated the number of cases required to reach proficiency and rated the role of prior multi-port robotic experience. Nine procedures were classified. Composite scores ranged from 8 (pyeloplasty, "slightly difficult") to 16 (radical cystectomy with intracorporeal diversion, "very difficult"). Estimated proficiency thresholds ranged from 10 to 33 cases. All experts considered prior multi-port robotic experience necessary before SP adoption. Early challenges were dominated by prolonged operative time, limited exposure and reduced ergonomics rather than instrument collision or spatial disorientation. We propose the first structured expert-based difficulty classification for SP robotic urological surgery. The procedural hierarchy mirrors historical laparoscopic and multi-port robotic classifications, supporting the concept that intrinsic complexity transcends the platform. This framework may inform training curricula, case selection during adoption and safe dissemination of SP robotic surgery.

items.title: Explainable AI-Driven Geospatial Intelligence for Resilient Distributed 6G Communication Systems
items.abstract: Emerging sixth-generation (6G) networks require intelligent, geographically aware communication systems capable of adapting to dynamic traffic, mobility, interference, and infrastructure failures. However, conventional network optimization often lacks spatial context, transparent decision-making, and coordinated resilience across distributed edge-cloud environments. This study proposes an Explainable AI-Driven Geospatial Intelligence Framework (EAGI-6G) to improve network reliability, resource allocation, and communication performance. The framework integrates geospatial information systems, distributed machine learning, digital network representations, and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). Geospatial features, including terrain, population density, mobility patterns, signal strength, and infrastructure locations, are fused with network telemetry to predict congestion, coverage degradation, and communication failures. A distributed learning architecture coordinates edge nodes and cloud services while minimizing centralized data dependence. Explainability methods, including SHAP and feature attribution, identify the spatial and network factors influencing decisions. Evaluation compares EAGI-6G against conventional geographic routing, centralized machine learning, distributed learning without geospatial features, and distributed learning without XAI. Key metrics include prediction accuracy, end-to-end latency, packet delivery ratio, network availability, recovery time, energy consumption, communication overhead, and explanation fidelity. The proposed evaluation targets measurable improvements over baseline methods: at least 10% higher failure-prediction F1-score, 15% lower end-to-end latency, 20% faster recovery, and 10% higher packet delivery ratio, alongside reduced energy consumption and communication overhead. These figures are research hypotheses, not experimentally established findings. Ablation studies will quantify the individual contributions of geospatial intelligence, distributed learning, and explainability under varying mobility, traffic, and failure scenarios. EAGI-6G establishes a testable framework for interpretable, spatially adaptive, and resilient 6G communication. Its comparative evaluation will clarify trade-offs among predictive performance, scalability, energy efficiency, transparency, and fault tolerance, supporting trustworthy network management for smart cities, connected infrastructure, and intelligent transportation. Keywords: distributed systems; Explainable Artificial Intelligence; Geospatial Intelligence; 6G communication; network resilience.

items.title: Exploring Lecturers' and Students' Perspectives on the Use of AI for Grammar, Vocabulary, and Pragmatic Development in Namibian Universities
items.abstract: This study examines the viewpoints of lecturers and students on the utilisation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to enhance grammar, vocabulary, and pragmatic skills in English and Applied Linguistics at Namibian universities. The research is based on the growing use of AI-powered writing tools such as ChatGPT, Grammarly, and QuillBot in higher education. Data were gathered via a qualitative interpretivist methodology through semi-structured interviews conducted with lecturers and undergraduate students at the Namibia University of Science and Technology (NUST) and the International University of Management (IUM). The study indicates that AI tools are seen as beneficial for augmenting grammatical correctness, broadening vocabulary, and strengthening pragmatic understanding in academic writing. Nonetheless, apprehensions pertaining to excessive dependence, academic integrity, and insufficient institutional guidance were also recognised. The study indicates that although AI possesses considerable educational potential, its implementation requires organised support, policy frameworks, and active participation to ensure effective learning outcomes.

items.title: Exploring the integration of artificial intelligence into residency education curriculum: qualitative interviews
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes more prevalent in medical practice, the importance of integrating AI curricula into postgraduate medical education (PGME) grows. While frameworks outlining necessary AI competencies for physicians exist, there is little consensus on how these competencies can be effectively implemented at the PGME level. Understanding the barriers and enablers to AI curricular integration is essential in preparing residents for an AI-enabled healthcare system. This study aims to explore expert perspectives on the ethical, institutional, and process-related challenges of integrating AI into PGME curriculum. Methods We conducted a qualitative study using an interpretive descriptive approach. Twelve physicians involved in AI and medical education across North America participated in semi-structured virtual interviews. Participants were recruited using purposive and snowball sampling. Interviews were audio-recorded and transcribed. Interview transcripts were analyzed using applied thematic analysis, with independent dual coding and consensus-based refinement of a structured codebook. Reflexive memos and analytic discussions supported rigor. Results Twelve interviews were completed; recruitment concluded at a pragmatic stopping point once successive interviews were judged to be converging on a consistent set of issues. Five major themes emerged: (1) the need for curricular agility in the face of rapid AI evolution, (2) gaps in faculty expertise, (3) limited institutional and regulatory readiness, (4) the role of nationally endorsed curricular standards, and (5) cultural resistance related to professional identity and responsibility. Participants emphasized prioritizing modular competencies, adopting co-learning models to address faculty limitations, and seeking clearer guidance from governing bodies. Conclusion Our findings offer practical guidance for educators on integrating AI into PGME curriculum. Building agile content, investing in multidisciplinary faculty development, fostering institutional and regulatory readiness, establishing national standards, and addressing cultural shifts can help PGME programs responsibly deploy AI curricula. In doing so, programs can position their graduates as reflective, ethical, and advanced clinicians capable of safely employing AI to improve patient care.

items.title: Exploring The Use Of Generative AI In Planning, Content, And Evaluation Of Learning Among University Lecturers
items.abstract: This study examines the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) among Indonesian university lecturers across three instructional domains: learning planning, content development, and assessment. It also investigates whether AI adoption levels differ across these domains and whether adoption intensity influences usage patterns. A quantitative within-subjects design was employed, involving 306 university lecturers with prior experience using generative AI in teaching. Data were collected through a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed using descriptive statistics and repeated-measures analysis of variance (RM-ANOVA), following appropriate statistical assumption tests. The findings reveal relatively similar levels of AI use across the three instructional domains, with no statistically significant differences between them (p = 0.551). However, significant differences were identified between lecturers with high and low levels of AI adoption (p < 0.001), indicating consistently greater AI use among high-adoption lecturers across all domains. Furthermore, no significant interaction was found between instructional domains and adoption levels (p = 0.560). These findings suggest that the intensity of individual AI adoption plays a more prominent role in determining usage patterns than the specific instructional domain. The study highlights the importance of strengthening lecturers' AI competencies, particularly in prompt design, output verification, and ethical use, alongside institutional support to promote responsible and pedagogically meaningful AI integration in higher education.

items.title: Financial Inclusion and Institutional Resilience in AI-Driven Islamic Finance: A Contract-Based Risk Governance Framework
items.abstract: The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Islamic finance has complicated the allocation of responsibility when financing decisions depend on automated assessments. This study develops a conceptual governance framework by reconstructing the complementary functions of Kafalah, Wakalah, and rahn. Using a qualitative doctrinal-comparative approach, it examines the contracts individually and through three pairwise relationships, then maps their functions to AI-related risks and institutional controls. The analysis identifies Kafalah–rahn as a mechanism for coordinating guarantees and collateral, Kafalah–Wakalah for linking guarantee obligations with accountable delegation, and Wakalah–rahn for governing delegated collateral activities. These relationships inform a five-layer architecture covering contractual authority, contingent risk allocation, collateral risk mitigation, technological governance, and maqāṣid al-sharīʿah-based evaluation. An illustrative financing scenario shows how model validation, human oversight, decision traceability, and proportionate safeguards may operate together. The framework distinguishes responsible financial access from institutional resilience without assuming that either outcome follows automatically. Its contribution is conceptual, and practical effectiveness requires subsequent expert and institutional assessment.

items.title: From Automation to Educational Value: A Conceptual Framework for Human–AI Co-Learning in Education
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in education has increased the availability of personalized learning, intelligent tutoring, generative feedback, and automated instructional support. However, technological capability does not necessarily translate into educational value. This conceptual study addresses the question: Under what pedagogical, human, and institutional conditions does AI capability translate into educational value? A critical conceptual synthesis of research on AI-supported personalization, intelligent tutoring, generative AI, cognitive engagement, learner and teacher agency, reliability, equity, and learning authenticity was undertaken. The analysis distinguishes AI capability from educational value and identifies five dimensions through which AI-supported education can be evaluated: personalization, reliability, human agency, equity, and learning authenticity. Based on these dimensions, the study develops a Human–AI Co-Learning Framework (HACLF) comprising six interconnected layers- learner, AI assistant, teacher, learning environment, governance, and society- and proposes the AI Education Value Index (AEVI) as a conceptual evaluation framework. The conceptual synthesis indicates that the educational consequences of AI are conditional on how technological capabilities are pedagogically integrated and mediated by human judgment, verification practices, equitable access, and authentic learner participation. The study contributes an education-centred perspective that shifts evaluation from what AI can automate to the conditions under which AI can support meaningful learning. HACLF and AEVI provide a basis for future empirical research and validation of AI-supported educational practices.

items.title: From Institutions to Neighborhoods: Designing an Intergenerational Care Community: A Service Design Proposal for Shared Living Between Children in Residential Care and Older
items.abstract: Care environments have traditionally been organized around institutional models that separate vulnerable populations from everyday community life. While these structures provide essential protection and professional support, their spatial organization and social routines may unintentionally reinforce identities based on dependency and institutional belonging rather than personal identity, autonomy, and social participation. Drawing on environmental psychology, social ergonomics, attachment theory, and service design perspectives, this research investigates how spatial configurations and relational structures influence the perception and experience of care environments. It explores the limitations of traditional care models and identifies the importance of small-scale environments, relational continuity, and opportunities for informal interaction. Based on these findings, the project proposes a service design model for an intergenerational living compound integrated within a residential neighbourhood. The proposed model consists of small house-like units where seniors, orphans in residential care, and stable adult figures coexist while maintaining privacy, autonomy, and personal boundaries. Shared spaces within the compound extend beyond residents by inviting the surrounding community to participate, creating opportunities for voluntary encounters between children, adults, and seniors. This proposal explores how spatial and organizational conditions can enable meaningful connections to emerge naturally. By transforming care environments from isolated institutions into open relational ecosystems, this research contributes to the exploration of how service design and architecture can support belonging, identity reconstruction, and more inclusive models of social care.

items.title: From Prompt to Polygon: Evaluating End-to-End Human–AI Workflows for Web-Based Generative 3D Authoring
items.abstract: Prompt- and image-driven 3D generation can lower the interaction barrier to digital asset creation, yet model-level advances do not establish whether non-specialists can operate a complete authoring workflow. This study designed and evaluated a web-based human–AI prototype integrating a React interface, FastAPI services, ComfyUI workflow orchestration, asynchronous job processing, persistent asset storage, and browser-based 3D visualization. We implemented four modes: Text-to-3D, Text-to-3D with ControlNet, Single Image-to-3D, and Multi Image-to-3D. Evaluation combined 14 requirement-derived black-box scenarios, cross-viewer GLB compatibility checks in three viewing environments, 35 completed generation jobs, task-based observation with seven participants completing 84 task executions, System Usability Scale (SUS) responses from a separate group of 12 students, and one expert assessment of implementation and output quality. All 14 functional scenarios produced the expected outcomes, and the tested GLB outputs opened in the integrated viewer, Blender, and 3dviewer.net. Mean server-side turnaround was 66.15 s; an exploratory Kruskal–Wallis test indicated differences among the observed workload distributions (H(3) = 10.52, p = .015, ε² = .243), but did not support causal or pairwise speed claims. All observed tasks were eventually completed, but only 61 of 84 executions (72.62%) were independent; Tasks 5 (enter Studio) and 10 (find the generated model in My Projects) each required assistance for five of seven participants. Mean SUS was 81.67 (SD = 9.25; 95% CI [75.79, 87.55]), while generated-model quality received a diagnostic expert score of 3.50/5. The study contributes an end-to-end human–AI authoring architecture and a multidimensional evaluation logic that separates functional conformance, deployment turnaround, cross-viewer compatibility, observed interaction, perceived usability, and output quality. Findings support the feasibility of accessible web-based generative 3D authoring while identifying discoverability and geometric-quality constraints.

items.title: From Signal to Biological Meaning: A Systematic Review of Construct-Validity Evidence for External Training Load Metrics in Sport
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: External training load (ETL) metrics describe external work but often imply metabolic demand, neuromuscular load, tissue stress, fatigue, or adaptation. These interpretations require construct-validity evidence beyond device accuracy or reliability. METHODS: We searched MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, and Academic Search Ultimate from inception to March 2026; final searches were on 1 March, except Embase on 7 March. Eligible peer-reviewed English studies evaluated an ETL indicator and its interpreted construct in athletes or physically active participants. Reports limited to technical accuracy, reliability, measurement error, or descriptive monitoring were excluded. We adjudicated one page-anchored construct-evidence chain per study. Measurement-property analyses used review-adapted COnsensus-based Standards for the selection of health Measurement INstruments (COSMIN); prediction models used the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool plus Artificial Intelligence (PROBAST+AI); other designs used Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) tools. Conceptual and methodological heterogeneity across metrics, target constructs, comparators, and study designs precluded meaningful meta-analysis; therefore, we used evidence maps and narrative synthesis. RESULTS: Forty-six studies contributed 46 primary evidence chains. Main study samples ranged from 7 to 71 participants, with smaller analysis-specific subsamples; most studies included only men. Construct attribution was explicit in 14 studies and explicit but qualified in 26; four were implicit but qualified and two reverse-target. Thirteen studies (28%) used a direct construct-matched criterion. Alternative proxies supported 16 studies (35%), condition or group contrasts 11 (24%), and mixed routes six (13%). General exercise intensity was the most frequent construct family (15 studies, 33%). Appraisal identified common limitations in hypotheses testing and analysis. Nineteen studies (41%) explicitly distinguished technical performance from construct interpretation, and 12 (26%) explicitly justified comparator selection. CONCLUSIONS: Most ETL metrics were supported as descriptions of external movement, work, or exposure rather than direct indicators of biological demand or response. Biological interpretations require an explicit construct, plausible mechanism, directional hypothesis, and construct-matched reference. Heterogeneity and methodological limitations reduce confidence in biological interpretations.

items.title: From Soft-Law AI Ethics to Risk-Based Public Sector AI Procurement: Recalibrating Malaysia’s Post-PDPA Governance Model
items.abstract: Public-sector artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly acquired through procurement rather than developed entirely in-house. This shifts a central governance question from whether public institutions endorse ethical principles to whether those principles become enforceable duties across the system life cycle. Malaysia has introduced national AI governance and ethics guidance and public-sector AI adoption guidance, while the Personal Data Protection (Amendment) Act 2024 recalibrates parts of the data-protection framework. Yet privacy compliance and high-level ethical principles alone cannot fully govern the acquisition and operation of AI used in public administration. This article asks how Malaysia can translate soft-law principles and existing legal duties into procurement controls proportionate to risk. Using doctrinal legal analysis and functional comparison with the European Union’s AI Act, the OECD AI Principles, UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of AI, Canada’s Directive on Automated Decision-Making, and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, it develops a normative Risk-to-Contract Accountability Framework (RCAF). The framework links risk classification to six controls: pre-award disclosure; impact assessment; contractual auditability; contestability and human review; incident reporting and material-change control; and continuing monitoring, remedies, and exit. The contribution is not a claim that AI procurement has never been studied, but a Malaysia-specific legal design connecting governance principles to the contract as a practical instrument of public accountability. The article argues that procurement should allocate responsibilities before deployment, preserve the authority’s ability to scrutinise supplier claims, and prevent contractual arrangements from insulating consequential decisions from review.

items.title: Future directions on integrated wildlife monitoring based on non-invasive approaches in Europe
items.abstract: Abstract The growing trend of emerging diseases at the wildlife-livestock-human interface underscores the need to establish integrated surveillance strategies within a One Health framework. In Europe, Integrated Wildlife Monitoring (IWM) tends to focus on specific pathogens, often with limited spatial and temporal scope. In this perspectives article, we address some of the most recent technological advances that could strengthen future IWM programs, with special emphasis on non-invasive approaches for monitoring wildlife populations and pathogen communities. We analyse the potential complementarity of different monitoring tools, such as camera traps, unmanned aerial vehicles, acoustic recording, and especially the detection of environmental nucleic acids (ENAD) using next-generation sequencing techniques, for the simultaneous characterization of pathogen and host communities. Despite the potential of molecular tools for large-scale monitoring, the lack of methodological standardization, the limited capacity to obtain quantitative information (e.g. population abundance or pathogen prevalence), and the difficulty of inferring the epidemiological significance of findings (e.g. whether molecular detection indicates viable pathogen) remain key challenges that limit their application. Finally, we argue that integrating these technologies with artificial intelligence (AI) represents a promising approach for managing large, heterogeneous datasets and developing proactive early warning systems. Moving toward the implementation of standardized and harmonized strategies that integrate ecological and epidemiological information should be a priority in European health surveillance frameworks. Strengthening coordination among surveillance systems by incorporating multi-source, AI-supported approaches will be key to improving early detection capacity and supporting evidence-based decision-making in addressing the global emergence of diseases.

items.title: GAILC AI Liability Exposure Map (ALEM): Identifying Potential AI Liability Exposure Before Harm Occurs—An Eight-Domain Framework for Preventive Examination
items.abstract: The GAILC AI Liability Exposure Map (ALEM) is an eight-domain analytical framework developed by the Global AI Liability Consortium (GAILC) to support the preventive identification and investigation of potential AI liability exposure before harmful consequences occur. As artificial intelligence becomes integrated into consequential organizational decisions and autonomous workflows, existing governance arrangements may not fully resolve questions about decision authority, meaningful human intervention, reliance on AI-generated outputs, operational execution, evidentiary sufficiency, and responsibility across multiple actors. ALEM addresses these questions through eight interconnected exposure domains: Authority Exposure Intervention Exposure Reliance Exposure Execution Exposure Allocation Exposure Evidence Exposure Consequence and Harm Exposure Change and Autonomy Exposure The working paper establishes domain definitions, distinguishing diagnostic questions, classification boundaries, evidence requirements, and a qualitative triage procedure for prioritizing preventive examination. A constructed AI-assisted financial approval workflow demonstrates the application of all eight domains, including three illustrative triage dispositions: Immediate Examination, Priority Remediation, and Routine Monitoring. The framework draws upon established research concerning human–automation interaction, automation bias, effective oversight, and accountability. It also provides conceptual cross-references to the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, ISO/IEC 42001, the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act, and the United Kingdom Senior Managers and Certification Regime. Two practical appendices provide a preliminary assessment worksheet and a proposed assessor-consistency evaluation protocol. ALEM forms part of GAILC's Preventive AI Liability Readiness approach and connects to the GAILC Intervention Test, Allocation Test, AI System Liability Self-Check, and AI Liability Exposure Brief. The framework is presented as a foundational analytical contribution intended for practitioner application, independent examination, and future methodological refinement. Its classification reliability and predictive validity have not yet been independently established. Core principle: The map identifies conditions that warrant investigation. It does not declare that legal liability exists. items.title: GenAI use duration, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep-onset difficulty among medical students in Shanxi, China: a cross-sectional survey
items.abstract: The widespread popularity of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has changed the learning and lifestyle of medical students, while its association with mental health status and sleep problems among medical students remains insufficiently. This study aimed to analyze the correlation between GenAI usage, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep-onset difficulty. A cross-sectional survey design was adopted in this study. Participants were medical students recruited from four medical universities in Shanxi, China, and data were collected via an online questionnaire. The usage duration of GenAI, anxiety and depressive symptoms, and sleep-onset difficulty were self-reported. Multiple logistic regression and linear regression analysis were performed to explore the association between GenAI use, anxiety, depressive symptoms, and sleep-onset difficulty. A total of 1,882 valid questionnaires were collected from medical students. After adjusting for all covariates, high-duration GenAI use was associated with increased odds of anxiety symptoms (OR = 2.02, 95%CI:1.48–2.77, P for trend < 0.001), high-duration GenAI use exhibited higher odds of sleep-onset difficulty based on the PSQI sleep latency component (OR = 1.67, 95%CI:1.26–2.24, P for trend < 0.001), compared to low/non-users. High-duration GenAI use was associated with elevated depressive scores (β = 0.66, 95%CI: 0.15–1.17, P for trend < 0.01) but not depressive symptoms. GenAI is widely used among medical students in Shanxi, China, and high-duration of GenAI is associated with anxiety symptoms and sleep-onset difficulty. Future research should deploy longitudinal design to clarify the long-term associations between GenAI use duration, mental health, and sleep problems.

items.title: Generation of synthetic clinical text: a systematic review
items.abstract: Generating medical synthetic text represents an effective solution for clinical NLP issues like sparsity and privacy. This paper conducts a systematic review on synthetic clinical text generation by formulating quantitative analysis to three research questions concerning the generation’s purpose, generation techniques, and the evaluation methods. We searched four databases including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Web of Science for publications associated with the topic and identified 87 relevant articles out of 1148. Results showed that the generation purposes were dedicated to Trustworthy, Medical Assistance, and Language Resource themes. Prompting LLMs was the main source of synthetic text (40 articles). GPTs were the main predominant technique used to generate the text (63 articles), especially ChatGPT (47 articles). Additionally, there were four main aspects of evaluation, including similarity, privacy, structure, and utility, where utility was the prevailing method for assessment (52 articles). The synthetic medical text empowered data augmentation and clinical documentation. Using text alteration, controlling real text portions, and federated learning, generative models can produce privacy-preserving medical text. This accelerates the development of new digital health applications.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI IN EFL SPEAKING AND PRONUNCIATION PRACTICE: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF CHALLENGES AND MITIGATIONS
items.abstract: While the role of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing instruction has received growing research attention, its impact on speaking and pronunciation remains underexplored. This PRISMA-based systematic review examines the challenges associated with using GenAI tools, particularly large language model (LLM)-based chatbots, for EFL speaking and pronunciation practice and synthesizes evidence-based mitigation strategies. Twelve studies that met the eligibility criteria yielded 48 challenges. These were organized into six thematic categories, including technical, pedagogical, learner-related, and equity concerns. The studies also varied in research design and instructional context. Several recurrent patterns emerged across the categories. Output accuracy and reliability represented the most persistent challenge and were linked to concerns about learner trust and uncritical reliance. AI-generated feedback was also repeatedly described as mechanical, formulaic, and lacking contextual sensitivity, highlighting a tension between the accessibility and scalability of these tools and limitations in areas that are important to learners. The studies commonly identified a human-in-the-loop approach as a key mitigation principle, alongside technical improvements and pedagogical interventions, including prompt literacy training. However, important questions remain unresolved, particularly whether GenAI reduces or increases teacher workload and if these tools narrow or widen existing equity gaps. Overall, the findings suggest that effective integration of GenAI into EFL speaking instruction requires attention to technical design, pedagogy, and institutional support, while several aspects of its implementation remain insufficiently understood.

items.title: Generative AI in Elementary Teacher Education: Opportunities, Risks, and Professional Ethics
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may influence how prospective elementary school teachers design, implement, and evaluate learning. It can support idea generation, lesson planning, differentiated activities, assessment rubrics, and reflective practice. However, fluent outputs are not necessarily accurate, developmentally appropriate, unbiased, or aligned with the curriculum and local sociocultural contexts. This article synthesizes the pedagogical opportunities, risks, and professional-ethical implications of GenAI use in Indonesian elementary teacher education and proposes directions for responsible integration. The study employs a narrative literature review based on exploratory searches of SciSpace, journal-publisher websites, academic sources, UNESCO publications, and Indonesian education-policy documents. The core literature covers 2020–2026, complemented by relevant foundational theory. The thematic synthesis identifies potential benefits for lesson planning and differentiation, alongside risks involving hallucinations, bias, developmental inappropriateness, privacy, copyright, unequal access, and cognitive overdependence. Responsible use requires AI literacy beyond prompt writing, including critical evaluation, ethical judgment, transparency, and accountability. The article proposes the KONTEKS framework as a guide for contextualizing, verifying, adapting, and taking responsibility for GenAI outputs. As a narrative review, it does not claim exhaustive systematic coverage or quantitative effect estimates; its recommendations require empirical testing in Indonesian elementary teacher education programs

items.title: Generative AI in Professional Learning at a Chinese Private Vocational College: Student Experiences and Teacher Perspectives
items.abstract: GenAI is now part of ordinary study for many students, but frequent use does not automatically mean deeper learning. This mixed-methods study examined professional-course use of GenAI at a private vocational college in Jiangxi Province, China. The evidence came from 431 student questionnaires and written responses from 18 teachers. After response-quality screening, 184 cases were retained for the primary quantitative analyses; 203 moderately screened cases and the full 431 responses were used for sensitivity checks. Meaningful learning engagement (MLE) was measured with two items and is therefore treated as a brief indicator of cognitive engagement rather than a validated multidimensional scale. Students reported using GenAI most often for knowledge clarification (82.6%) and coursework or exercises (74.5%); practical-training use was lower (20.7%). Perceived professional value (PPV) was associated with MLE (β = .550). When PPV and MLE were entered together, both remained associated with post-adoption learning experience (PAE; β = .339 and β = .364, respectively). The standardized indirect association from PPV to PAE through MLE was .200, with a 95% bootstrap CI of [.109, .307]. These cross-sectional results describe associations rather than causal effects. Teacher accounts added important context. Teachers valued GenAI for quick explanations but also described answer-oriented use, inaccurate professional content, weak links with practical training, and uncertainty about institutional guidance. They wanted more discipline-specific examples, clearer expectations, and assessment that made student reasoning visible. Across both strands, three tensions stood out: efficiency versus engagement, general usefulness versus professional fit, and rapid student adoption versus slower institutional response. Because the evidence came from one college, the findings should be interpreted as context-specific.

items.title: Generative AI in Southeast Asian TVET: A Systematic Review of Learning Outcomes, Ethics and Research Directions
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT entered technical and vocational education and training faster than evidence on their effects. Objective: This review synthesized empirical evidence on the applications, learning outcomes and ethical challenges of generative artificial intelligence in Southeast Asian vocational education. Method: Following PRISMA 2020, ten search strings were run in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar for 2022–2026, which yielded 254 unique records, of which 25 primary studies met the eligibility criteria. Findings: The studies came from Indonesia (17), Malaysia (5) and Thailand (3), and 18 were published in 2026. Fourteen concerned English language learning. Four quasi-experimental studies reported gains in writing, speaking, writing self-efficacy and AI literacy, while most other evidence was self-reported, and no study measured hands-on technical competence. Academic integrity (9 studies), overreliance (7) and inaccurate output (5) were the most frequent risks, and privacy and unequal access were also reported. Benefits depended on teacher mediation, task design, AI literacy and institutional guidance. Implications: Institutions should favors guided over unrestricted use, and research should prioritize controlled, longitudinal studies with practical assessment. Contribution: The review offers the first region-specific evidence map and a framework for responsible integration.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Dentistry: Clinical Applications, Evidence, Limitations, Ethical Considerations, and a Framework for Responsible Implementation
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including large language models (LLMs) and multimodal foundation models, is increasingly being used in dentistry, dental education, and scientific research. Unlike conventional predictive AI, which is generally developed for defined classification or prediction tasks, GenAI can produce new text, images, summaries, and other outputs from user prompts. In dentistry, potential applications include patient communication, clinical documentation, education, literature synthesis, and selected forms of decision support. These applications are accompanied by important risks, including hallucinated information, bias, privacy breaches, fabricated references, and automation bias. This narrative review summarizes recent evidence on GenAI in dentistry, with emphasis on the distinction between assistive use and autonomous clinical decision-making. Recent systematic, scoping, and narrative reviews describe applications in dental education, oral and maxillofacial surgery, implant dentistry, endodontics, and other areas, but the available evidence remains heterogeneous and prospective clinical validation is limited. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) may improve evidence alignment by linking language models to curated external sources, although dental-specific evidence remains early. Based on the reviewed literature, responsible implementation should be task-specific and should include data minimization, verification of outputs, human accountability, documentation, and ongoing monitoring. A seven-stage framework is proposed: define the task, assess risk, protect data, verify output, retain human decision-making, document relevant AI use, and monitor performance. At present, GenAI is best regarded as an assistive technology that can support, but should not replace, professional dental judgment.
